blocks.text: A fitter gets a nut off the shelf that spins freely onto a bolt for two turns and then jams solid. Both are marked M12, but one is 1.75 mm pitch and the other 1.25 mm. The designation was incomplete, and the drawing never said which.

blocks.markdown: A **screw thread** is a helical ridge on a cylinder. Its geometry is described by a few quantities: the **major diameter** $d$ (the largest diameter of an external thread, the nominal size), the **minor diameter** (the smallest), and the **pitch** $P$, the axial distance between adjacent thread crests. For a single-start thread each full turn advances the nut by one pitch, so axial advance equals number of turns times $P$.

blocks.title: ISO metric thread designation
blocks.text: The designation **M10 x 1.5** means: metric thread (M), major (nominal) diameter 10 mm, pitch 1.5 mm. A designation with no pitch, such as **M10**, means the standard **coarse** pitch for that diameter. Additional symbols, such as 6g, give the tolerance class.

Preferred metric coarse and typical fine pitches

blocks.title: Interpreting a designation
blocks.prompt: Interpret M12 and M12 x 1.5. How far does a nut advance in 5 turns on each, and how many pitches fit in a 30 mm length of the fine thread?

steps.text: M12 with no pitch is the coarse thread: d = 12 mm, P = 1.75 mm (from the table). M12 x 1.5 is the fine thread with P = 1.5 mm.
Advance in 5 turns for the coarse thread.
Advance in 5 turns for the fine thread.
Pitches in 30 mm of the fine thread.

blocks.answer: Coarse advances 8.75 mm and fine 7.5 mm in 5 turns; the fine thread has 20 pitches in 30 mm.

blocks.markdown: **Conventional representation.** Drawing every helix is impractical, so threads are drawn by convention. **External thread** (a bolt or stud): in the side view the **major diameter** is a thick continuous line and the **minor diameter** a thin continuous line, usually drawn at about 0.85 d; the thread length ends with a thick line. In the end view, the major circle is thick and the minor circle is a thin arc of about three quarters of a circle. **Internal thread** (a tapped hole), in section: the **minor diameter** (the bore) is thick and the **major diameter** thin; hatching runs up to the thick minor-diameter line. In the end view, the thick circle is the minor diameter and the thin three-quarter arc is the major diameter.

rows: Thick major circle, thin 3/4 minor arc
Thick minor circle, thin 3/4 major arc

blocks.title: Thin line for an M20 bolt
blocks.prompt: An M20 bolt is drawn with the usual rule that the thin minor-diameter line is at 0.85 d. Give the diameter of the thin line and the pitch implied by M20 alone.

steps.text: M20 with no pitch is coarse: P = 2.5 mm.

blocks.answer: The thin line is drawn at 17 mm diameter and the implied pitch is 2.5 mm.

blocks.markdown: **Coarse and fine pitch.** Coarse threads (the default) have deeper teeth, assemble quickly, tolerate dirt and minor damage, and are better in soft materials such as aluminium. **Fine threads** have a smaller pitch, a shallower tooth and a larger minor diameter and so a slightly larger tensile area. They are preferred for **thin-walled parts** (less material removed), for **fine adjustment** (small advance per turn), and where **vibration** might loosen the joint (a smaller helix angle gives more self-locking).

blocks.title: Say the pitch if it is not coarse
blocks.text: The designation without a pitch is coarse. Any fine thread must carry its pitch, for example M12 x 1.5, or the wrong part may be made.

items: Read the letter M, then the nominal diameter, then the pitch.
Draw the major diameter thick and the minor thin for an external thread; reverse for the internal thread in section.
Draw the three-quarter arc in the end view.
Use fine pitch for thin walls, adjustment and vibration.

points: M10 x 1.5 means metric, 10 mm major diameter, 1.5 mm pitch; no pitch means coarse.
Threads are drawn by convention: thick major and thin minor on an external thread, reversed for an internal thread in section, with a three-quarter arc in the end view.
Coarse is the general default; fine pitch suits thin walls, fine adjustment and vibration.

questions.stem: What does the designation M16 x 1.5 mean?
questions.explanation: M is metric, 16 is the nominal major diameter and 1.5 is the pitch. The coarse M16 would be 2.0 mm pitch.

questions.stem: In the side view of an external thread, which diameter is drawn as the thick line?
questions.explanation: For an external thread the major diameter is the outline, thick, and the minor diameter is thin. The convention is reversed for an internal thread in section.

questions.stem: A single-start M10 x 1.25 screw is turned 6 full turns. Calculate the axial advance, in mm.
questions.explanation: Advance = N x P = 6 x 1.25 = 7.5 mm. A coarse M10 would advance 9 mm in the same turns.

questions.stem: An M16 bolt is drawn with the thin minor-diameter line at 0.85 d. Calculate the diameter of that thin line, in mm.
questions.explanation: 0.85 x 16 = 13.6 mm. This is a drawing convention, not the exact minor diameter.

questions.stem: In an end view of an internal thread (a tapped hole), which line is the thin three-quarter arc?
questions.explanation: In an internal thread the minor diameter is the bore, thick, and the major diameter is shown as a thin arc about three quarters of a circle. The convention is the reverse of the external thread.

questions.stem: A drawing note reads M24 with no pitch stated. Which pitch is implied?
questions.explanation: A designation with no pitch is the coarse series, and the coarse pitch of M24 is 3.0 mm. 1.5 mm and 2.0 mm are fine pitches for that diameter.

questions.stem: A thin-walled tube is to carry an external thread and needs fine axial adjustment against vibration. Which thread is best?

options.text: A coarse thread, because it is quicker to assemble
A fine thread, because it removes less wall and advances less per turn
Any thread, since pitch does not matter
A coarse thread, because it has a larger minor diameter

questions.correctOptionText: A fine thread, because it removes less wall and advances less per turn

distractorRationale.d: Coarse has the smaller minor diameter.

questions.explanation: Fine pitch has a shallower tooth so less wall is cut away, a smaller advance per turn for adjustment, and better resistance to loosening. Coarse threads are deeper, not larger at the minor diameter.

questions.stem: Describe how an external thread is drawn in the side view and the end view using the conventional representation, naming the line types.
markingGuide: Side view: thick major, thin minor line (about 0.85 d)
Thread length ends with a thick line
Thin three-quarter arc for the minor diameter
questions.explanation: A complete answer names all four details, with line types, for the external thread. Each point in the marking guide earns credit, so state every point explicitly and give its reason.

questions.stem: Explain the difference between M10 and M10 x 1.25, give a design reason to choose fine pitch, and state what is wrong with drawing only M10 where a fine pitch is required.
markingGuide: M10 is coarse, pitch 1.5 mm; M10 x 1.25 is fine
Reason: thin wall, adjustment or vibration resistance
Without pitch the coarse thread is assumed, so the wrong thread would be made
Fine pitch must be stated explicitly
questions.explanation: Credit for the pitch values, a valid reason for fine pitch and the risk of omission. Each point in the marking guide earns credit, so state every point explicitly and give its reason.

questions.stem: A fine-pitch thread has more threads per unit length than a coarse thread of the same diameter.
questions.explanation: Smaller pitch means more crests in each millimetre of length. The tooth is also shallower.
